frase_gancho.texto: A clay altar shaped like a theater, built to speak with the ancestors.

puente_narrativo.texto: To close out the hall, look for the animals that accompanied the gods of Teotihuacán: jaguars, snakes, coyotes, and birds, which peek out from murals and vessels. It is the last corner before you leave the city.

guion_corto.texto: This is a incense burner of the kind called “theater type,” one of the most characteristic clay creations of Teotihuacán. It stands seventy-six centimeters tall and was found in 1911 by the archaeologist Manuel Gamio in Azcapotzalco. It has two parts: a conical bowl for burning copal and, behind it, a chimney covered by a façade like a stage. At the center is the mask of a figure, a deified ancestor, with large ear ornaments. Around it are plaques made with molds: butterflies, birds, shields, flowers, and tassels. It is a portable altar, designed for speaking with the dead through smoke, in the courtyard of a house or in a neighborhood temple.

guion_largo.texto:
Its story begins in 1911 in Azcapotzalco, today part of Mexico City, dozens of kilometers from Teotihuacán. There Manuel Gamio carried out a layer-by-layer excavation, considered one of the first in Mexico to use that method: he worked from the top down and recorded each level. It showed something that seems obvious today: that beneath the Mexica layer there were older ones, and that Teotihuacán had left its traces outside its own valley.

The name “theater” is not ancient; archaeologists gave it. The chimney looks like a curtain or a stage: two side pillars, a stepped crown on top and, in the middle, a niche where the figure peers out. In reality it was an altar. In the bowl below, copal was burned, the smoke rose through the chimney and came out at the back, and the face seemed wrapped in a cloud.

The most surprising thing is how it is made. The butterflies, birds, shields, and flowers were not modeled one by one: they were made with molds and attached in series, like the pieces of a construction set. It is a kind of mass production from about one thousand five hundred years ago. That indicates that there were workshops that made these altars for many homes, and that the religion of Teotihuacán was also a trade with specialists.

Braziers like this have been found in neighborhoods and dwellings, not only in temples. They were part of the cult of the ancestors: each family, each neighborhood, kept the memory of its dead alive with smoke and offerings. It is a version of Teotihuacán that fits in a courtyard. And it reminds us that the city was not only pyramids and rulers, but also ordinary people with an altar at home.

The symbols that surround the mask are military and cosmic: butterflies with open wings, which centuries later the Mexica would associate with the souls of dead warriors; quetzal feathers; shields with darts. Some people read a message in them: the ancestor is also a warrior and a protector. What is burned is resin; what is asked for is protection.

Copal, the resin of a tree, is still used in Mexico in ceremonies and altars for the dead. In the ethnography halls upstairs you will see how that custom survives in communities today: the aromatic smoke that rises, the altar that is set up with care, the idea that the dead return to visit the living. The Teotihuacán incense burner is one of its ancestors.

Azcapotzalco holds another story. Centuries after Teotihuacán, it was the capital of the Tepanecs, a powerful lordship that dominated the Valley of Mexico. The Mexica paid it tribute, until in 1428 they rebelled and, allied with other peoples, such as the Texcocans of Nezahualcóyotl, the poet king whose name you already know, defeated their lord Maxtla. It was the beginning of the Mexica empire.

That means the place where this incense burner was found was present at two great moments in the history of the valley: the expansion of Teotihuacán and the birth of the Mexica empire. When you reach the Mexica Hall, remember that the history you will see there began, in part, in this very neighborhood.

texto: Find the mask of the figure at the center and its large ear ornaments
Count the butterflies and birds made with molds
Imagine the smoke rising through the chimney, behind the façade

texto.Dimensions: 0.76 m high x 0.414 m in diameter
texto.Discovery: Found complete in 1911 by Manuel Gamio in Azcapotzalco

texto.pregunta: Myth: “Theater-type” braziers were used to stage plays.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The name is modern, given because of their stage-like shape; they were altars where copal was burned for the ancestors.
